recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York
intro: “The Snow Is Dancing” is the fourth piece of Debussy’s Children’s Corner, in which small rapid notes pass between the pianist’s hands. Debussy set a slow melody against this figuration, and at the close the figuration rises towards the top of the keyboard.

sections.label: A · Alternating semiquavers around a slow tune
sections.mNote: Alternating semiquavers surround a slow tune.

sections.label: B · Triplets against the accompaniment
sections.mNote: Repeated upper notes sound against the accompaniment

sections.label: A′ · Return of the alternating notes
sections.mNote: The alternating notes return and climb towards the treble.

cues.title: Alternating semiquavers and second melody
cues.text: The two hands alternate in semiquavers, each playing in the gaps left by the other. Debussy marks the piano doux et estompé (soft and blurred), though the notes are short. A slower melody in longer notes enters among them, marked doux et triste (soft and sad).
cues.evidence: Debussy, Children’s Corner, Durand (1908), plate D. & F. 7188, pp. 16–17: alternating semiquavers, doux et estompé, and the longer melody marked doux et triste. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Triplets in the treble
cues.text: Repeated notes in the treble fall into groups of three against the running accompaniment. Debussy marks Cédez un peu, then Au Mouvement. Sharply accented chords interrupt the figuration.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 18–19: repeated-note triplets, Cédez un peu, Au Mouvement and accented chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening pattern
cues.text: The opening alternating pattern returns molto pp. Its notes climb into the highest octaves, where Debussy writes perdendo (dying away). The score also marks Sans retenir.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 20–21: return of the alternating pattern, octave-up treble writing, molto pp e perdendo and Sans retenir.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Repeated triplets cross the running notes
transitions.from: A · Alternating semiquavers around a slow tune
transitions.how: The two hands briefly run down and up the piano. At Cédez un peu, the right hand takes up repeated triplets and the left continues in even semiquavers. Under Au Mouvement the treble line descends, and an accented chord marked sforzando falls across the pattern.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 18, second to fourth systems: running link, repeated triplets, Cédez un peu, Au Mouvement and sforzando.

transitions.title: Alternating figure returns over low D
transitions.to: A′ · Return of the alternating notes
transitions.how: The accented chords stop and a line of semiquavers runs alone, without accompaniment. The pattern then returns over a low D, with the hands alternating again and the original tune above. Debussy marks the return softer still, più pp.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 20: unaccompanied running link and return of the alternating figure over low D, marked più pp.

fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Debussy died in 1918 and the suite was published in 1908. This is territorial term reasoning for the composition, not worldwide clearance or a claim about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.value: Rule 3 — EU public-domain term basis for a phonogram published before 1963; territorial, not worldwide.
fields.note: The documented LP issue is dated 1951, establishing publication before 1963 independently of the 1950 session. Its earlier 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 1 November 2013 extension threshold. US sound-recording status is not established. No Creative Commons licence or worldwide public-domain dedication is claimed.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
